general.note: Short-grain rice, cooked the day before and chilled. Cold rice is what lets the grains separate.

optional.note: Ham or char siu, diced small and added with the rice.

tools.name: Wok
tools.note: A 24 cm frying pan works. It holds less heat, so cook one portion at a time and stir less.

tools.name: Rice cooker
tools.note: For the rice the day before. A pot with a lid does the same.

tools.name: Spatula
tools.note: A wok spatula or a ladle.

steps.title: Cook the rice ahead
points: Cook the rice the day before and spread it on a plate to cool.
Keep it uncovered in the fridge overnight so the surface dries.
In a hurry, spread hot rice thin and give it 20 minutes in the freezer.

steps.title: Prep everything
points: Slice the spring onion thin.
Beat the eggs with a pinch of the salt.
Break the cold rice up with wet hands until no lumps are left.

steps.title: Heat the wok
points: Set the wok over the highest heat until a drop of water skates and vanishes.
Pour in the oil and swirl it up the sides.
This takes longer than you think, usually 2 minutes.

steps.title: Scramble the eggs
points: Pour the eggs into the center and leave them for 3 seconds.
Break them into large soft curds with the spatula.
Stop while they still look wet. They finish cooking in the rice.

steps.title: Add the rice
points: Tip the rice straight onto the half-set egg.
Press it flat with the back of the spatula, count to five, then flip and press again.
Repeat until every grain is coated and loose, about 3 minutes.

steps.title: Season the rice
points: Scatter the rest of the salt and the white pepper from a height so it lands evenly.
Pour the soy sauce, and the Shaoxing wine if using, down the hot side of the wok, not onto the rice.
It hisses and goes in as smoke and smell rather than as a wet patch.

steps.title: Finish and plate
points: Toss the spring onion through and take the wok off the heat.
Add the sesame oil now, off the heat, so it keeps its smell.
Pack it into a bowl and turn it out onto a plate as a mound.

troubleshooting.problem: The rice is sticky and clumped
troubleshooting.solution: It was too fresh or too wet. Day-old chilled rice has a dry surface and comes apart under the spatula. Fresh rice steams in the wok and glues itself together.
It was cooked through before the rice went in. Take it to soft curds only, and remember the rice keeps cooking it for another 3 minutes.
The soy sauce went straight onto the rice. Pour it down the side of the hot wok so most of it flashes off as steam.
Usually salt, not soy sauce. Salt seasons the grains, soy sauce seasons the smell. Add a pinch of salt and a pinch of white pepper and toss again.

troubleshooting.problem: The wok never gets hot enough
troubleshooting.solution: Home stoves lose their heat the moment food lands. Cook one portion at a time, let the wok recover for 10 seconds between additions, and resist stirring constantly.

troubleshooting.problem: The rice sticks to the wok
troubleshooting.solution: The wok was not hot enough when the oil went in, or there was too little of it. Two tablespoons for one portion sounds like a lot and is the right amount.
Dice 40 g of ham or char siu and add it with the rice. Anything wetter than that, such as fresh vegetables, waters the rice down.
